source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection
finding: Introduced LOGIC, a 13-type fallacy dataset from online quiz sites, and LOGICCLIMATE, real climate news. Off-the-shelf zero-shot models (RoBERTa-MNLI, BART-MNLI, TARS, GPT-2, GPT-3) were near random.
numbers: LOGIC: 2,449 items, 13 types (Faulty generalization 18.01%, Ad hominem 12.33%, Ad populum 9.47%). LOGICCLIMATE: 1,079 items. 12 models tried, micro F1 from 8.62% to 53.31%. RoBERTa-MNLI 12.22 F1, GPT-2 13.67, GPT-3 12.00. Best fine-tuned: Electra 53.31, DeBERTa 50.29.
quote: existing pre-trained large language models perform poorly on this task
limits: Quiz-site sentences, not real arguments. GPT-3 got a plain label prompt in 2022. Best model still fails about half the time.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot detection of a named fallacy from the label word alone does not work; the agent should not trust a bare 'is this fallacious' judgement.

source: Jin et al. (2022) structure-aware classifier
finding: Masking content words so only the argument form remains, and pairing it with the standard logical form of each fallacy, beat the best plain language model.
numbers: Electra-StructAware 58.77 F1 vs Electra 53.31 (+5.46) on LOGIC; exact match 47.67%, 12.01 points above best plain model. LOGICCLIMATE direct transfer: Electra 22.72 F1, StructAware 27.23 (+4.51); after fine-tuning on climate 23.71 vs 29.37. Ablation: raw premise plus logical-form hypothesis 56.72.
limits: Form templates were taken from web pages. Transfer to real climate claims is weak (27 F1). Ablation shows the gain comes from the form-aware label text.
agent_relevance: Giving the model the form of the fallacy, not only its name, helps. Useful for a marked claim-type check block.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) Robust and Explainable Identification of Logical Fallacies in Natural Language Arguments
finding: Built a three-stage test (binary detection, coarse class, fine class) and tried case-based reasoning (instance and prototype), knowledge injection, data augmentation and curriculum learning with small fine-tuned language models.
numbers: Binary detection F1 98.4 to 99.7 percent (best: instance-based Electra-NLI). In-domain on LOGIC: coarse F1 82.7%, fine F1 62.7%. Out of domain on LOGIC Climate coarse: instance-based 46.6% vs prototype-based 57.3%; fine about 24%. More than 10 augmentation substitutions hurt.
limits: Binary task is easy because the fallacy and non-fallacy sets differ in style. Fine class and out-of-domain remain poor. Models are small encoders, not chat LLMs.
agent_relevance: Retrieving similar solved cases helps, but out-of-domain accuracy drops sharply. Do not expect a fallacy tagger to transfer to new text sources.

source: Alhindi et al. (2022) Multitask Instruction-based Prompting for Fallacy Recognition
finding: Unified five fallacy datasets (28 unique fallacies) with instruction prompts on T5. Multitask training beat single-dataset T5, BERT and few-shot GPT-3. Zero-shot UnifiedQA was useless.
numbers: Acc/macro-F1: T5-3B multitask Argotario 64/64, Propaganda 73/56, Logic 70/66, Covid-19 29/28, Climate 25/20. T5-large single-dataset: Argotario 25/14, Logic 56/45. GPT-3 few-shot: Argotario 45/39, Propaganda 19/13, Logic 20/22. UnifiedQA zero-shot Logic 8 macro-F1. Prompt with definitions beat names only in 4 of 5 datasets. Explanations in GPT-3 few-shot gave no gain.
limits: Fine-tuned models, not chat-tuned. Low scores on Covid and Climate (macro-F1 20 to 28). The same fallacy name means different things in different datasets (Red Herring).
agent_relevance: Definitions in the prompt help most for neighbouring fallacies; datasets disagree on what a label means, so the agent needs its own written definitions.

source: Payandeh et al. (2023) How susceptible are LLMs to Logical Fallacies? (LOGICOM)
finding: A persuader LLM debates a debater LLM on a claim. When the persuader (helped by a separate fallacy-writing agent) used fallacies, the debater was convinced more often than under sound reasoning.
numbers: Debater convinced by fallacious vs logical persuader: GPT-3.5 37% vs 29% of claims; GPT-4 67% vs 37%. Across all three repeats: GPT-3.5 17% vs 10%; GPT-4 56% vs 37%. Headline: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 convinced 41% and 69% more often. With sound reasoning the debater flipped from disagree to agree in 16.13% (GPT-3.5) and 20.25% (GPT-4) of debates. Dataset of over 5k logical vs fallacious argument pairs.
limits: Opinion flips on open controversial topics, no ground truth. The 41% and 69% headline does not follow directly from the quoted raw rates (37/29, 67/37), so a different base was probably used; trust the raw rates. Each claim run 3 times; GPT-3.5 is more inconsistent (20% of claims got one or two successes vs 10% for GPT-4). The stronger model was more, not less, susceptible.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a strong model is swayed by fallacious arguments in its input. Supports a marked block for appeals to authority or stated guesses, and a rule that quoted persuasion cannot change the answer alone.

source: Payandeh et al. (2023) LOGICOM ablation: helper agent
finding: Swapping the fallacious helper for a logical helper changed who won. For the GPT-4 debater, almost no claims were won only by the fallacious helper.
numbers: Claims won only with logical helper vs only with fallacious helper: GPT-3.5 17.66% vs 10.5%; GPT-4 28% vs 0.83%.
limits: Only one persuader prompt style. Three repeats per claim.
agent_relevance: A two-agent design (main task agent plus a separate helper for fallacy craft) is a working pattern; fallacy knowledge can also be used to red-team the agent's own draft.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: A Benchmark and Comprehensive Study of Fallacy Detection and Classification
finding: Merged existing fallacy sets into one taxonomy with 3 levels, 23 fallacy types, and a disjunctive annotation scheme that allows several valid labels. Measured models and humans zero-shot.
numbers: 9,545 unannotated texts; 200 annotated texts with 260 fallacy instances; 28% of 203 spans have two or more valid labels. F1 at Levels 0/1/2: random 0.435/0.061/0.010; GPT-3.5 0.627/0.201/0.138; Zephyr 7B 0.524/0.192/0.098; Vicuna 13B 0.557/0.173/0.100; LLaMA2 Chat 13B 0.549/0.160/0.096; Falcon 7B 0.397/0.130/0.022. Average human 0.749/0.352/0.186.
quote: Levels 1 and 2 are largely out of reach of LLMs in zero-shot settings
limits: Human baseline is only 4 annotators on 20 texts, and humans also scored low (Level 2 F1 0.186). Zero-shot, basic prompt, span level. Appeal to emotion hardest for humans and models.
agent_relevance: Even the best model trails people, and people disagree with each other. Fine labels are unreliable; the coarse level is the safe operating point for the agent.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: direct level prompting and annotator agreement
finding: Prompting directly at Level 1 made no real difference. Each human annotator's own work, used as gold, agreed poorly with the others.
numbers: Level 1 F1 prompted directly: Mistral Instruct 0.149, Zephyr 0.185 (vs 0.144 and 0.192 extrapolated from Level 2). Four user annotators scored Level 0 F1 0.616 to 0.696 and Level 1 0.253 to 0.310; the MAFALDA gold scored Level 2 F1 0.186 on average for humans vs best alternative 0.144.
limits: 20-sample human test. The disjunctive metric lets several labels count, so scores are not comparable to single-label benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Fine-grained fallacy label is partly a matter of taste, so a pipeline should accept more than one valid label.

source: Pan et al. (2024) Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers? (EMNLP 2024)
finding: Tested GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Qwen2.5, Llama3, Mistral and Llama2 with single-round and multi-round zero-shot prompts on 7 datasets, against fine-tuned T5 baselines.
numbers: Zero-shot GPT-4 beat fine-tuned T5-3B and T5-large on Argotario (best 78.94 macro-F1) and was close on Reddit (79.10 vs 83.20 and 80.42). LLMs beat T5 in all out-of-distribution holdouts. Multi-round prompts improved 83.7% of experiments; average gains 1.63 (GPT-4), 2.46 (GPT-3.5), 4.95 (Qwen2.5-14B), 3.67 (Qwen2.5-7B), 7.54 (Llama3-8B), 4.02 (Mistral-7B), 1.27 (Llama2-13B) points. GPT-4 on MAFALDA: informal definitions 48.38 vs formal 49.78 macro-F1.
limits: Long noisy-context data (Propaganda) stays near 33 to 35 macro-F1 for GPT-4. Few-shot GPT-4 on LOGIC: one-shot 54.48, two-shot 55.14 vs best zero-shot about 50.5. Multi-round prompts raise the rate of out-of-list answers.
agent_relevance: Prompt style matters less than model size; small models gain most from multi-step prompting. Fits a code-driven analyse-then-label pipeline.

source: Pan et al. (2024) multi-round schemes ranking
finding: Ranking of multi-round schemes by macro-F1: general fallacy analysis with warm-up round first, zero-shot CoT second, analysis alone third, then single-round with definitions, definition generation, no definitions, and premises-and-conclusion last.
numbers: Average ranks: GFA-W 4.13, CoT 4.33, GFA 4.35, With Definitions 4.65, Definition Generation 4.77, Without Definitions 4.90, Premises and Conclusion 5.84. Text: the warm-up round lowered the failure rate from 15.09% to 12.27%; CoT had a lower failure rate than both.
limits: Rank gaps among the top three are about 0.2. Free analysis before the label raises out-of-list answers because the model anchors on its first judgement. Human-written definitions beat self-generated ones.
agent_relevance: Forcing a premise-and-conclusion extraction first did not help; free analysis then a constrained label was best. Ask for the label from a fixed list in a separate code-checked step.

source: Jeong, Jang and Park (2025) LLMs Are Better Logical Fallacy Reasoners with Counterargument, Explanation, and Goal-Aware Prompt Formulation (NAACL Findings)
finding: Enrich each argument with a generated counterargument, explanation and goal, ask a validity question per enrichment, and rank answers by confidence. Works zero-shot and fine-tuned on 5 datasets, 29 fallacy types.
numbers: Macro-F1 gpt-3.5-turbo with prompt ranking vs plain zero-shot: Argotario 0.69 vs 0.41, Logic 0.32 vs 0.25, Covid-19 0.56 vs 0.14, Climate 0.58 vs 0.13. gpt-4 prompt ranking: Propaganda 0.20, Argotario 0.83, Logic 0.37, Covid 0.76, Climate 0.71 vs zero-shot 0.19, 0.50, 0.28, 0.25, 0.11. Zero-shot CoT (Kojima) with gpt-4: 0.20, 0.47, 0.28, 0.33, 0.12, no real gain. Headline: up to +0.60 F1 zero-shot, +0.45 fine-tuned.
limits: The ranking order added little: gpt-4 on Covid scored 0.85 with no ranking info, 0.71 with random order, 0.76 with ranking. Propaganda and Logic stay at 0.17 to 0.37. Explanation queries helped most, counterargument queries least.
agent_relevance: Asking why an argument might fail (explanation) and what the arguer wants (goal) is the useful part; zero-shot CoT alone did not help. Candidate S1 step: generate explanation and goal for a quoted claim, then query validity.

source: Jeong et al. (2025) query-type analysis on a small model
finding: With Llama2-7b, zero-shot was near floor and explanation or goal queries lifted it more than the ranking step did.
numbers: Llama2-7b macro-F1 zero-shot vs Explanation vs Goal vs Ranking: Logic 0.07 / 0.32 / 0.26 / 0.19; Covid 0.05 / 0.24 / 0.16 / 0.13 (as listed in the appendix table). Fine-tuned roberta-base with Explanation on Climate: accuracy 0.84, F1 0.74.
limits: Small model, noisy data; ranking sometimes hurt small models (Propaganda 0.08 to 0.06).
agent_relevance: Per-query enrichment is a cheap step; the combiner (ranking) is the weak part, and code-side vote counting is simpler.

source: Jeong et al. (2025) with Hong et al. (2024) DEF baseline
finding: A definition-enhanced prompt (DEF, Hong et al. 2024) was run as a baseline and gave only small, uneven gains over plain zero-shot.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo macro-F1 zero-shot / ZCoT / DEF: Propaganda 0.07/0.08/0.11; Argotario 0.41/0.39/0.48; Logic 0.25/0.23/0.22; Covid 0.14/0.11/0.11; Climate 0.13/0.13/0.09.
limits: Original Hong et al. 2024 paper not opened; numbers are the re-run in Jeong et al.
agent_relevance: Fallacy definitions alone are a weak lever; agrees with Alhindi that definitions help only close neighbours.

source: Li et al. (2024) Reason from Fallacy: Enhancing LLMs' Logical Reasoning through Logical Fallacy Understanding (NAACL)
finding: Built LFUD, a fallacy understanding dataset (WHAT, WHY, HOW; five tasks; 12 fallacy types plus correct sentences) with GPT-4. Fine-tuning on it raised four logical reasoning benchmarks, while the older LOGIC fallacy set did not.
numbers: LFUD: 4,020 instances (3,000 train, 1,020 test). LLaMA2-13B accuracy Origin vs Origin+LFUD: LogiQA2.0 45.55 to 47.90, Reclor 47.20 to 50.20, TaxiNLI 68.54 to 73.70, FOLIO 61.76 to 66.18. Origin+LOGIC: TaxiNLI 68.54 to 40.60 for LLaMA2-13B; LogiQA2.0 42.30 to 35.62 for LLaMA2-7B. Vicuna-7B FOLIO 50.49 to 56.37 with LFUD. GPT-4 scored 78.6 to 88.0 on LFU tasks; LLaMA2-7B 24.75 to 47.86, below random in places.
limits: Fine-tuning of 7B to 13B models, three runs averaged. LFUD is synthetic (GPT-4 written). Only GPT-4 correctly judged the 654 correct Big-Bench sentences; others labelled them fallacies to please the question.
agent_relevance: Teaching WHY and HOW (explain, then repair a fallacy) improves general reasoning, but plain labelled lists can hurt. Supports using the fallacy lens for repair, not only detection. No scaffold-level test.

source: Lei and Huang (2024) Boosting Logical Fallacy Reasoning in LLMs via Logical Structure Tree
finding: Build an unsupervised tree of connective words (because, therefore, but) and argument spans, from a constituency parse and a taxonomy of 10 logical relations, and feed it to LLMs as text or as soft-prompt embedding.
numbers: Abstract-level claim: up to 3.45% gain in detection and 6.75% in classification. Llama-2 on Logic classification accuracy 69.36 to 74.16 and F1 63.05 to 66.38 with the tree. GPT-3.5 Argotario classification F1 40.26 to 55.92; GPT-3.5 Logic classification F1 31.30 to 35.97.
limits: Gains are not uniform: RoBERTa Argotario detection F1 85.01 to 83.47 and Flan-T5 86.86 to 83.75 got worse with the tree. The soft-prompt version needs training.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-side step: extract connectives and clause pairs and show them to the model so it checks whether the stated relation (therefore, because) is supported. Fits the program-does-the-counting rule.

source: Lei and Huang (2024) per-model detail
finding: GPT-3.5 used as a plain classifier lagged fine-tuned encoders on detection; the connective tree helped GPT-3.5 and the Logic set most.
numbers: Detection F1 on Argotario: GPT-3.5 75.14 vs 82.29 with tree. Logic classification macro-F1: GPT-3.5 31.30 to 35.97; RoBERTa 60.03 to 64.30; Flan-T5 63.60 to 69.37.
limits: Table layout in the paper text is garbled, so cells were matched by row order; direction of the Logic gains is clear.
agent_relevance: Structure help is largest for the weakest model and the fine-grained Logic set.

source: Zhou, Westerdijk and Islam (2025) Joint Effects of Argumentation Theory, Audio Modality and Data Enrichment on LLM-Based Fallacy Classification
finding: Qwen-3 8B classified six fallacies from US presidential debates with a base prompt, a Pragma-Dialectics prompt and a Periodic Table of Arguments prompt, with text only, plus context, plus audio-derived emotional tone. More input usually made results worse.
numbers: Accuracy text-only / +context / +context+audio: base 51/49/46, Pragma-Dialectics 53/49/46, Periodic Table 44/45/25. Base prompt macro-F1 49 text vs 47 context. Base prompt missed 95% of Slippery Slope. With audio tone, Appeal to Emotion recall went 80 to 95% in the base prompt (65 to 90% in the PD prompt).
quote: basic prompts often outperformed enhanced ones
limits: Small 8B model, six classes, hand-balanced small sample (5% recall steps suggest about 20 items per class), single run. Theory prompts helped by only about 2 points.
agent_relevance: Adding emotional-tone or context metadata biases the label toward that cue (emotion): a concrete input leak. Supports keeping tone and context out of the judging step.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) per-class effects
finding: Per-class numbers show which fallacies are fragile to extra input.
numbers: Base prompt F1 text/context/context+audio: Appeal to Emotion 33/31/29; Appeal to Authority 48/42/45; Ad Hominem 81/77/78. Slippery Slope recall 5% in base prompt. Periodic Table prompt recall for Slogans 40/37/2.
limits: About 20 items per class; changes of 3 to 5 points are within noise.
agent_relevance: Slippery slope and slogans are nearly missed by an 8B model; do not rely on LLM tagging for these types.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Socrates or Smartypants: Testing Logic Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs with Logic Programming-based Test Oracles (SmartyPat-Bench)
finding: New benchmark of 502 real Reddit posts with subtle fallacies plus a Prolog-based fallacy generator. Every model over-flagged fallacies with near-zero misses. Reasoning models did not beat non-reasoning ones on detection but were better at naming the type.
numbers: 502 posts chosen from 2,500 reviewed; three fallacy types make up 79.7% of the manual data, three rare ones 1.77%. Models include Claude 3.7, GPT-o3-mini, DeepSeek R1, DeepSeek V3, Grok-2 (nine models). All models: high false-positive rate, near-zero false-negative rate; reasoning models more false positives. Example: Claude 3.7 flagged 'If you are a beginner, it is best to begin with a flat board' as a fallacy.
quote: reasoning models tend to overanalyze, flagging benign content as fallacious
limits: Per-model F1 values are in figures and were not read as exact numbers. Facts for the generator were produced by Claude.
agent_relevance: Models over-detect: they assume a fallacy is present. A fallacy flag should never veto content alone; require a second, code-checked criterion.

source: Xu et al. (2025) rule-guided categorization
finding: Giving the model the formal rule of the fallacy improved naming the type, while long free reasoning chains hurt detection.
numbers: In the label-score table starred rows (with the Prolog rule) scored higher than unstarred rows for most classes, e.g. DeepSeek R1 with rule reached 100 on one class vs 50 without; DeepSeek V3 with rule 70 vs 38 without.
limits: Numbers read from a garbled figure table; use for direction only.
agent_relevance: Supplying the explicit logical rule of each fallacy (as in Jin 2022) gives a similar benefit for chat models; fits a name-the-form-then-check operator.

source: Lim and Perrault (2024) Evaluation of an LLM in Identifying Logical Fallacies: A Call for Rigor When Adopting LLMs in HCI Research
finding: GPT-4 classified labelled texts into 7 common fallacies (with a None option). Accuracy was good on the subset the authors cared about.
numbers: Full set accuracy 0.79, precision 0.76, recall 0.66, F1 0.71. Subset excluding invalid or unidentified: accuracy 0.90, precision 0.87, recall 0.89, F1 0.88. 11% of Questionable Cause items were labelled Hasty Generalization; 12% of another class labelled Red Herring.
limits: Seven well-known fallacies, one prompt design; the authors chose the subset for their use case, so 0.90 is a favourable framing. Test-set size 780 was taken from the web summary, not checked in the text.
agent_relevance: Seven coarse, well-known classes give usable accuracy in GPT-4. Reporting accuracy so users can calibrate trust is a sensible pattern for the agent's output.

source: Zhai et al. (2025) RuozhiBench: Evaluating LLMs with Logical Fallacies and Misleading Premises
finding: 677 trick questions containing fallacies or false premises (English and Chinese). 17 LLMs from 5 series answered; best was far below people.
numbers: Best model Claude-3-haiku 62.00 average score, Mixtral-8x22B 58.99, Llama-3.1-70B 57.78; humans above 90%. Larger models beat smaller ones within every series. Judge agreement: Claude vs GPT Pearson 0.568, large disagreement 3.99%; Claude vs Llama large disagreement 50.37%.
limits: LLM-as-judge ratings (low agreement for Llama as judge). Questions are puns and trick logic, not textbook fallacy lists.
agent_relevance: Models accept false premises inside the question. Supports a premise-check step on the input before answering.

source: Habernal, Wachsmuth, Gurevych and Stein (2018) Before Name-calling: Dynamics and Triggers of Ad Hominem Fallacies in Web Argumentation
finding: Used Reddit Change My View rule-violation labels as ad hominem ground truth. Ad hominem is rare there, and the theory's five sub-types did not fit real data well.
numbers: Crowd labels on 100 args: Cohen kappa 0.79 (six workers, MACE 0.9). Crowd gold vs moderator labels accuracy 0.878 (human upper bound). Bi-LSTM 0.782, CNN 0.810 accuracy on 7,242 balanced instances. Only 0.2% of CMV posts are ad hominem vs 19.5% of comments under news articles. 41% of 200 args labelled abusive by 16 workers each; tu quoque, circumstantial and guilt by association had very low agreement. Crowd found 11 ad hominem the moderators missed.
limits: Old neural models (2018). One community with strict rules. The theoretical type split fails on long mixed attacks.
agent_relevance: Theory-based fallacy sub-types are not reliably separable in real text; use coarse types. Pre-LLM classifiers approach human level only on the binary task.

source: Habernal et al. (2017) Argotario: Computational Argumentation Meets Serious Games
finding: A game where players write fallacious arguments of a given type, guess the type in opponents' arguments, and get crowd-graded, producing labelled fallacy data. Five types plus a non-fallacy class.
numbers: Types: ad hominem, appeal to emotion, red herring, hasty generalization, irrelevant authority, plus non-fallacious. Gold labels by MACE with at least four extra player votes. Soft vs hard feedback study: 20 and 17 participants, Mann-Whitney U, soft feedback had no significant negative effect on experience.
limits: Demo paper; data quality analysis deferred. Small user study. The data later became standard benchmark data for the LLM papers above.
agent_relevance: Writing a fallacy on purpose is a teaching device that could also generate adversarial inputs to test the agent's input filter.

source: Payandeh et al. (2023) LOGICOM design as an agent loop
finding: The benchmark is itself an agent loop: a persuader plus a separate fallacious helper, debate rounds, and a final agree/disagree readout, repeated three times per claim.
numbers: Three repeats per claim and scenario. A long fallacy prompt in the persuader distracted it from debating, which is why a helper agent was added.
limits: Single-claim readout is a binary opinion, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Splitting roles (fallacy craft in a helper, main task in the main agent) is an existing use; a fallacy-checking helper for S1 is the natural reverse.

source: Cross-paper summary of fallacy datasets in LLM work (Alhindi 2022; Jeong 2025)
finding: Across papers the same five datasets recur (Argotario, Propaganda, LOGIC, Covid-19, Climate) and scores vary far more by dataset than by model.
numbers: gpt-4 zero-shot macro-F1 (Jeong): Propaganda 0.19, Argotario 0.50, Logic 0.28, Covid-19 0.25, Climate 0.11. T5-3B multitask (Alhindi) macro-F1: Propaganda 56, Argotario 64, Logic 66, Covid 28, Climate 20.
limits: Label sets differ (5 to 18 types) and metric conventions differ, so cross-paper numbers are not strictly comparable.
agent_relevance: Plan the agent's fallacy check around a small fixed label list tied to its own task, not around generic benchmark labels.
